narr: One of the most significant flooding events in years occurred during November 11th and 12th, given both the amounts of rainfall and the footprint where flooding occurred. In the wake of high pressure passing east off the mid-Atlantic coast, a plume of deep tropical moisture was rapidly carried inland to the central Appalachians ahead of a slow-moving cold front. Though this plume was of tropical origin, it was not directly related to Tropical Storm Eta, which was off the coast of southern Florida. Precipitable Water values were in the extremely high range of 1.9 to 2.2 inches with this airmass, around the 99th percentile for mid-November. In addition, evapotranspiration was significantly lower than during the previous few months given lower daytime heating and the fact that most vegetation had become dormant for the upcoming winter months. Despite dry conditions for almost two weeks leading up to the event, numerous instances of flooding and flash flooding occurred as 4 to 6 inches of rain fell across portions of the Piedmont on the 11th, followed by an additional 1 to 3 inches on the 12th. Some of the activity was convective in nature, producing locally 2 to 4 inch per hour rainfall rates. The rainfall produces numerous instances of flooding and flash flooding, followed shortly by river flooding.
ev: After 2 to 3 inches of rain fell across Appomattox county during the morning, an additional 1.75 to 2.25 inches of rain fell during the evening, most of it within a hour, as a line of slow-moving thunderstorms passed across the area. This caused numerous creeks, already running high from the earlier rainfall, to flood out of their banks. Notable among the flood reports was water about one foot deep running across Horseshoe Road. At least five water rescues were performed by emergency personnel, including one at North Creek Road where North Creek was observed flooding the roadway, and another at River Ridge Road at the Appomattox River. Additional rounds of rain of weaker intensity persisted through the late evening hours, maintaining the flooding conditions, though flash flooding ended by 11:00 pm.

Runoff from 1 to 1.5 inches of rain in about a one-hour time period caused flooding several inches deep to flow across the intersection of Wilkerson Road and Kentuck Road. The road was reported impassible until after the water receded.

After 2 to 2.5 inches of rain fell during the morning across much of Buckingham County, a band of slow-moving thunderstorms moved across the county during the evening. Runoff from this heavy rain caused water to flow across the road near the intersection of Howardsville Road and Watoga Road.

After 2 to 2.5 inches of rain fell during the morning across much of Buckingham County, a band of slow-moving thunderstorms moved across the county during the evening. Runoff from this heavy rain caused water to flow across the road near the intersection of Twin Creek Road and West James Anderson Highway.

With 1.5 to 2 inches of rain having already fallen earlier in the day, a band of fast-moving thunderstorms producing heavy rain moved across the community of Blacksburg. Between 7:00 pm and 7:40 pm, a weather station in Blacksburg recorded about 1.25 inches of rain with this band. Runoff from the rainfall push Stroubles Creek out of its banks near the Duck Pond on the Virginia Tech University campus, flooding Duck Pond Drive. The road was impassible for several hours.

With about 2 inches of rain having already fallen earlier in the day across the Jacobs Creek watershed, a band of thunderstorms passed across the area during the evening. Multiple personal weather stations observed 1.25 to 1.5 inches of rain during a 45-minute period between 6:30 pm and 7:15 pm, falling over saturated soils. Runoff from this rain pushed Jacobs Creek out of its banks, which was then observed flowing across Red House Road. The road was impassible until the flood waters receded. An automobile became stranded in the floodwaters and had to be towed out.
